'''Eblaite''' ({{IPAc-en|ˈ|ɛ|b|l|ə|.|aɪ|t|,_|ˈ|iː|b|l|ə|-}},<ref>{{cite Dictionary.com|Eblaite}}</ref> also known as '''Eblan [[ISO 639-3]]'''), or '''Palaeosyrian''',{{sfn|Garbini|1981|p=81}}{{sfn|Lipiński|2001|p=51-52}} is an extinct [[East Semitic language]] used during the [[3rd millennium BC]] in [[Upper Mesopotamia|Northern Syria]].<ref name="archi">{{cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=F2SRqDzB50wC&pg=PA313 |title=Concise Encyclopedia of Languages of the World |first1=Keith |last1=Brown |first2=Sarah |last2=Ogilvie |page=313 |year=2010 |publisher=Elsevier |isbn=978-0-08-087775-4 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171018002349/https://books.google.com/books?id=F2SRqDzB50wC&pg=PA313 |archive-date=2017-10-18}}</ref> It was named after the ancient city of [[Ebla]], in modern western [[Syria]].<ref name="archi" /> Variants of the language were also spoken in [[Mari, Syria|Mari]] and [[Tell Brak|Nagar]].<ref name="archi" />{{sfn|Lipiński|2001|p=52}} According to [[Cyrus Gordon|Cyrus H. Gordon]],<ref name=gordon>{{cite book |first=Cyrus H. |last=Gordon |author-link=Cyrus H. Gordon |title=Amorite and Eblaite |page=101}}</ref> although scribes might have spoken it sometimes, Eblaite was probably not spoken much, being rather a written [[lingua franca]] with East and West Semitic features.

The language was discovered through [[cuneiform]] tablets found in Ebla.

== Discovery ==
[[File:Syrie 3mil aC.svg|alt=Map of Ebla and other principal sites of Syria and Upper Mesopotamia in the second half of the third millennium BC|left|thumb|Ebla and other principal sites of [[History of Syria#Ancient Near East|Syria]] and [[Mesopotamia]] in the second half of the third millennium BC.]]
The 1964 discovery at the [[Ebla|Tell Mardikh]] site in Northern Syria of an ancient city from the second half of the third millennium BC completely altered archaeological knowledge of the time, as it indicated the existence of a contemporary urban culture during the [[Early Dynastic Period (Mesopotamia)|Early Dynastic Period]] of [[Mesopotamia]], within a geographic zone where, at the time, previous excavations had revealed nothing on the same scale.

In agreement with [[Ignace Gelb]]'s theories on the subject of all inhabited centers in Syria of the same era, it appeared that the Tell Mardikh civilization's cultural identity did not necessarily fall within the [[Semitic people|Semitic]] family.<ref>"Our sources pertaining to the West Semites in Syria and Palestine flow almost uninterruptedly from the Old Babylonian period on. Two important conclusions can be drawn on the basis of the study of geographical names and of other, less important considerations : 1) The Semites entered Syria in mass in the Old Babylonian period, encountering a population of unknown, but certainly not Hurrian ethnic affiliation. 2) The Semites must have been established in Palestine long before the Old Babylonian period, and nothing prevents us from assuming that they may have been native to the area from time immemorial." In I. Gelb, 1961 b, p. 45</ref> However, in 1968, the discovery at the same site of a statue bearing an ancient [[Akkadian language|Akkadian]] inscription, mentioning the king [[Ibbit-Lim]] of [[Ebla]], soon contradicted this hypothesis.<ref>See Giovanni Pettinato, 1967–1968.</ref> It therefore became possible not only to identify this city as the ancient city of Ebla, referred to in numerous Mesopotamian and Egyptian sources, but additionally, considering the strong linguistic connotations of the king's name,<ref>M. Liverani, 1965</ref> to specify the identity as [[Amorites|Amorite]]. It became necessary, however, to revise these conclusions again, after the 1974 discovery in the ancient ruins of a [[Bronze Age]] palace (2400–2225 BC) of 42 [[cuneiform]] [[Clay tablet|tablets]], then of 17,000 others the following year, revealing a language different from [[Amorite language|Amorite]], which exhibited archaic morphological characteristics present in Akkadian, with incontestable lexical similarities to [[West Semitic languages]] such as [[Hebrew language|Hebrew]] or [[Aramaic]]. [[Excavation (archaeology)|Excavations]] were directed by Professor [[Paolo Matthiae]] and the inscriptions translated by [[Giovanni Pettinato]].

This opposition between a West Semitic [[lexicon]] and an Akkadian [[Morphology (linguistics)|morphology]] led to controversies surrounding the nature of this language. For P. Fronzaroli, the opposition suggested an Akkadian [[dialect]] that had undergone a strong Western influence.<ref>P. Fronzaroli, 1977, p.40</ref> On the other hand, Giovanni Garbini favored a more nuanced approach, drawing attention to the fragility of a comparison with Akkadian, and pointing out that there is no other contemporary model with which to draw comparisons. In his "Considerations on the Language of Ebla", he highlighted the artificial character of this opposition between morphology and lexicon and noted that "Akkadian differs from Western Semitic as we knew it hitherto because the latter was documented only on the phase following Amorite innovation. If it is traced back to the time before these innovations, a northwestern pre-Amorite Semitic begins to emerge, which is concordant with Akkadian just because the latter preserved its earlier character after Amorite invasion".{{sfn|Garbini|1981|p=79}} Essentially basing his study on the lexicon, G. Pettinato was nevertheless the first to announce in 1975 the discovery of a new Semitic language, to which he gave the name "Paleo-[[Canaanite languages|Canaanite]]."<ref>G. Pettinato 1975, pp. 361–374</ref> Although the academic community was in favor of this idea, they were not unanimous regarding Pettinato's proposed name. In fact, while indicating advantageously its similarity to [[Hebrew language|Hebrew]], [[Ugaritic]], or [[Phoenician language|Phoenician]], the name proved nevertheless incapable of indicating its morphological roots in [[East Semitic languages]]. G. Garbini then proposed the term "Paleo-[[Syriac language|Syrian]],"<ref>G. Garbini 1984, pp. 65–68</ref> but again, this proved just as inadequate to convey the Mesopotamian particularities and was not accepted. Therefore, without a name to fit this new language's different linguistic characteristics, "Eblaite" was finally chosen.

=== Nature of the documents ===
Of the Eblaite corpus, whose publication began in 1974 as stated above, the majority of discovered documents are administrative or economic in nature, along with about a hundred historical tablets as well as some scholastic writings: [[lexicon]]s, [[Syllabary|syllabaries]], or bilingual texts. To this list, we must also add a few rare literary texts: fragments of [[myth]]s, [[Epic poetry|epics]], [[hymn]]s, [[proverb]]s, as well as some documents for [[Evocation|conjuration]].

From a linguistic perspective, although a great number of these documents were effectively written in [[Sumerian language|Sumerian]], a rather large portion of these only used the language [[ideogram]]matically, as confirmed by certain [[Semitic languages|Semitic]] elements added to the [[Sumerogram]]s – such as morphological [[Marker (linguistics)|markers]], suffix pronouns, or certain prepositions – which reveal an underlying language distinct from Sumerian.{{center|''in'' U<sub>4</sub> [[Dingir|DINGIR]] ''a-mu-su''<sub>3</sub> NIDBA
"the day when the god of his father had his festival"
}}Such writing practices obviously made approaching Eblaite difficult. Fortunately, some rare documents, bilingual letters or tablets, mostly written syllabically, enabled the breaking down of this graphical barrier and the clarification of our knowledge of this language.

Of course, even if we add to this collection the [[Onomastics|onomastic]] material, which in Semitic languages typically consists of short sentences, the portion of the Eblaite corpus that is usable from a [[Linguistics|linguistic]] perspective remains relatively narrow and limited from a [[Morphology (linguistics)|morphological]], [[Syntax|syntactical]], or [[Lexicology|lexical]] point of view.

=== The graphical barrier and writing practices ===
The main difficulty faced by those studying the language of Ebla arose largely from issues in the [[writing system]]. Indeed, Eblaite shares its [[cuneiform]] writing system with the [[Sumerian language|Sumerian]], [[Akkadian language|Akkadian]], [[Hittite language|Hittite]], [[Hurrian language|Hurrian]], and [[Elamite language|Elamite]] languages, a graphical system where each symbol may have collectively or separately an [[ideogram]]matic and/or [[Phoneme|phonetic]] value. In the first case, the symbol or chain of symbols simply signifies an idea that is understandable by way of its Sumerian meaning; in the second case, the symbol indicates, with a more-or-less large approximation based on writing practices, the form of an Eblaite term following a principle of syllabic decomposition.

The comparative study of Eblaite symbols reveals some differences with the systems used by other schools of [[scribe]]s. On the other hand, the Eblaite syllabary, without being identical, bears significant similarities with that of the ancient Akkadian used in [[Kish (Sumer)|Kish]] during the [[Early Dynastic Period (Mesopotamia)|Early Dynastic Period]] (DA II).

In fact, three transcription practices appear in the Ebla texts: one exclusively syllabic, another using both syllabism and ideography, and the last largely employing the ideographic principle. Included in the first category is mostly the incantatory texts and the writing of [[Anthroponymy|anthroponyms]]; in the second, the epistolary, historical, and literary documents, not to mention some diplomatic texts; and in the third, economic and administrative texts, relating to the management and stewardship of the palace where [[Ideogram|ideography]] is a sufficient system for the writing of ''realia''. Qualitatively and quantitatively, this situation entirely resembles that of the [[Mesopotamia]]n corpus.

Only a small portion of documents found are syllabic, compared to the large quantity of texts written using [[Sumerogram|Sumerian]] [[logogram]]s.<ref>Huehnergard, John. “Reading Ancient Mail.” Journal of the American Oriental Society, vol. 138, no. 4, 2018, pp. 691–707</ref> This led G. Pettinato<ref>R.B. I., 25. 1977, p. 238</ref> to consider, at first, that these documents were written in Sumerian. Such a hypothesis obviously no longer holds today with regard to our understanding of the writing and formulation practices particular to Sumerian and Eblaite scribes. These graphical conventions are so specific that they are very often sufficient to identify the language underlying the ideograms.<ref>I. Gelb, 1977, p. 7</ref> Thus, for example, the Sumerian practice of writing filiation following the formula <small>X DUMU Y</small> ("X son of Y") stands out from the Akkadian and Eblaite practice which prefers the phrasing <small>X DUMU.NITA Y</small>.<ref>I. Gelb, 1981, pp. 13–14</ref>

However, if, as we just saw, we can identify a [[Signified and signifier|signified]] of Semitic origin beneath a Sumerogram, it remains difficult to extract its signifier. Fortunately, the restoration of phonetic values to these symbols has been made possible by the existence of bilingual lexical lists, where each Sumerian ideogram has its Eblaite form specified in a glossary using syllabic writing.

Even when the phonetic value of the word is specified, a whole series of [[Semantics|semantic]] problems remains, still obstructing our understanding. For example, when an Eblaite scribe uses the symbol <small>[[Lugal|LUGAL]]</small> meaning "king" in Sumerian, he transcribes it with its Akkadian value ''šarrum'' but translates it as "dignitary." This simple example shows the gaps in interpretation that may result from reading Eblaite symbols while only considering their Sumerian values.

As for the strictly syllabic system of writing, it is not free of issues either. The rarity of Vowel + Consonant -type symbols (VC) require certain approximations in the transcription of words. Thus we find the term ''ʾummum'' "mother" syllabically rendered as ''u<sub>3</sub>-mu-mu''. Additionally, while Sumerian sometimes proceeds morphologically by reduplication of a word to make it plural, Eblaite reuses this practice with the same meaning, but transforming it into a simple graphical signified. In this way we find forms along the lines of nasi<sub>11</sub>-nasi<sub>11</sub> to write the plural of nas<sub>11</sub> "the people." Furthermore it is not uncommon that the writing presents a defective character, where all the morphological markers are not indicated: ''ḫa-za-an'' šu-ba-ti = *''ḫazānum'' ''yimḫur'' "the mayor takes it."<ref>G. Pettinato, ''Catalogo dei testi cuneiformi di Tell Mardikh'' (MEE 1, 1979) no. 6424-30</ref>

To these issues we can also add those connected with the intrinsic limits of the Sumerian writing system, incapable of rendering a portion of Semitic languages' [[Phonology|phonological]] system. As Diakonoff specifies, the Sumerian system is organized upon a tense~lax opposition and can only with great difficulty render the voiced~unvoiced opposition as well as the [[Emphatic consonant|emphatics]] of Semitic languages. Thus we find the syllables /da/, /ṭa/, and /ta/ transcribed with the same symbol DA, as well as the syllables /gu/, /ku/, and /qu/ with the same symbol GU.

For the same reasons, it is equally impossible for the Sumerian writing system to render the [[Laryngeal theory|laryngeals]] and [[Pharyngeal consonant|pharyngeals]] of Eblaite. However, to overcome these difficulties, they used – just like ancient Akkadian – graphical conventions such as the use of the symbols E and MA to render the [[phoneme]]s /ḥ/ or /ʿ/, or else by playing on syllabic symbols which end in the vowel /e/, which is nothing but the [[Vowel|vocalic]] trace of one of the two preceding articulations.

Additionally, as shown by the written forms ''la-ḫa'' for /''laḫān''/ or ''ba-da-a'' for /''baytay''/ for example, the phonemes /w/, /y/, /m/, and /n/ are not rendered graphically in the final or initial position. Taking these two examples again, notice that, for one, the quantity of the vowels is not rendered by the writing (the form ''da-za-a'' for /''taṣṣaʾā''/ "they will go out" shows us that double consonants face the same fate) and secondly, that the vowel /a/ is used equally to represent the syllables /ʾa/, /ya/, and /ay/.

== Phonological system ==
As shown above, the difficulties with reading Eblaite texts complicate approaching its [[Phonology|phonological]] system.

Studying the usage context for the symbols I, I<sub>2</sub>, A, ʾA, ḪA, etc. with regard to the writing conventions of Akkadian scribes enabled the determination, beyond some identification difficulties created by the graphical barrier, of "the existence and autonomy of the [[phoneme]]s /h/, /ḥ/, and /ḫ/ confirmed by the [[Realization (linguistics)|realization]] of the vowel /a/ as [ɛ] in the closed syllables /ḥaC/ and /ʾaC/, as well as the tendency to extend this phenomenon to the vowel /a/ followed by a [[Pharyngeal consonant|pharyngeal]]. It is currently lacking the elements to determine the existence of a phoneme /ġ/ or a variant [ġ]."<ref>P. Fronzaroli, 1978, p. 137. Translated from the French: "l’existence et l’autonomie des phonèmes /h/, /ḥ/ et /ḫ/ que confirme la réalisation de la voyelle /a/ en [ɛ] dans les syllabes fermées /ḥaC/ et /ʾaC/, de même que la tendance à étendre ce phénomène à la voyelle /a/ suivie d’une pharyngale. On manque actuellement d’éléments pour juger de l’existence d’un phonème /ġ/ ou d’une variante [ġ]"</ref>

Also through a contextual analysis of the symbols z + Vowel (V): ze<sub>2</sub>, s + V: se<sub>11</sub>, š + V, Pelio Fronzaroli confirmed the existence of the phonemes /s/, /ṣ/, /ḍ/, and /ẓ/, as well as the phonemes /s/, /š/, and /ṯ/, a group to which it is perhaps also necessary to add /z/.<ref>Ibid, pp. 137–139. See also P. Fronzaroli, 1980, pp. 65–89 in ''Studi Eblaiti'' 1</ref>

As for the existence of [[diphthong]]s, this remains questionable. The diphthong /ay/ seems to be conserved in Eblaite as illustrated by the form /ʿayn-ʿayn/ though it is still preserved in other semitic languages which have lost the diphthong. However, the reality of this phoneme is heavily discussed by I. Gelb: "The main difference between Fronzaroli's treatment of the diphthong /aj/ at Ebla and mine is that Fronzaroli believes (...) that the original diphthong /aj/ was preserved in Eblaite (even though not written), while I take it to have developed to /ā/."<ref>I. Gelb, 1981, p. 24</ref>

Here we should also highlight the issue of the unstable realization of [[Liquid consonant|liquids]] with the alternation of /r/ and /l/. I. Gelb speculated two reasons for this phenomenon: "If the weakness of the r / l phoneme (which is amply exemplified at Ebla) should be considered as an indication of the [[Hurrian language|Hurrian]] influence on Eblaic phonology, then we should note that this feature is characteristic not only of Hurrian (and other languages in the general area), but also of [[Egyptian language|Egyptian]], and may therefore be either a surviving feature of the [[Afroasiatic languages|Semito-Hamitic]] (or Afro-Asiatic) or a cross-linguistic areal feature."<ref>Ibid. p. 65</ref>

== Pronominal system ==
Eblaite has two forms of [[personal pronoun]]s: independent and suffix. Additionally, the texts have also revealed a [[Determiner|determinative pronominal]] form as well as [[Interrogative word|interrogative]] forms. The [[Epigraphy|epigraphical material]] does not always allow a complete reconstruction of the paradigms, and the gaps must be filled on the basis of linguistic comparisons as well as internal reconstitutions that take the language's own structures into account.<ref>[https://books.google.com/books?id=xUyVEAAAQBAJ&pg=PA70] Hasselbach-Andee, Rebecca. "Eblaite and Akkadian: A Look at the Pronominal System." Bēl Lišāni: Current Research in Akkadian Linguistics (2022): 70</ref>

== Nominal system ==
Eblaite presents a [[Nominal (linguistics)|nominal]] system that is comparable to that of Akkadian and whose traces are found in certain Semitic languages. In particular, there are three [[inflection]]al categories: [[Grammatical gender|gender]], with masculine and feminine forms; [[Grammatical number|number]], with singular, dual, and plural; and finally [[Grammatical case|case]], covering both syntactical relationships like the [[Nominative case|nominative]], [[Accusative case|accusative]], and [[Genitive case|genitive]] cases, but also more concrete relationships like the [[Dative case|dative]] and [[Locative case|locative]] cases.<ref>M. Diakonoff prefers the terms "dative-locative" and "locative-adverbial," rather than the conventional "dative" and "locative," in order to better cover the semantic range of these cases. See Diakonoff, 1990, p. 25</ref> This organization of the nominal morphology was likely that of all Semitic languages until the first millennium BC.

== Verbal system ==
Eblaite's [[verb]]al system follows the same structure as that of other Semitic languages, where the paradigmatic framework is organized based upon a double axis: the derivational axis, within which the verb's basic form goes through a certain number of modifications, and the inflectional axis, where the verb takes on an [[Grammatical aspect|aspectual]], [[Grammatical person|personal]], or [[Grammatical mood|modal]] value through a system of [[suffix]]ation and [[prefix]]ation.

== Classification ==
Eblaite has been described as an [[East Semitic language]] or a "North Semitic" language; scholars notice the great affinity between Eblaite and pre-Sargonic [[Akkadian language|Akkadian]] and debate the relationship between the two.

=== East Semitic classification ===
*Scholars such as [[Richard I. Caplice]], [[Ignace Gelb]] and [[John Huehnergard]] have the view that Eblaite is an East Semitic language not to be seen as an early Akkadian dialect,<ref>{{cite book|url= https://books.google.com/books?id=aWhHAQAAQBAJ&pg=PA7|title= The Semitic Languages|author= Robert Hetzron|page= 7|year= 2013|publisher= Routledge|isbn= 978-1-136-11580-6|url-status= live|archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20160506133340/https://books.google.com/books?id=aWhHAQAAQBAJ&pg=PA7|archive-date= 2016-05-06}}</ref> because the differences from other Akkadian dialects are considerable.<ref name="arol">{{cite book|url= https://books.google.com/books?id=3hc1Yp0VcjoC&pg=PA259|title= The Study of the Ancient Near East in the Twenty-first Century: The William Foxwell Albright Centennial Conference|author= Jerrold S. Cooper, Glenn M. Schwartz|page= 259|year= 1996|publisher= Eisenbrauns|isbn= 978-0-931464-96-6|url-status= live|archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20180320153250/https://books.google.com/books?id=3hc1Yp0VcjoC&pg=PA259|archive-date= 2018-03-20}}</ref>
*[[Manfred Krebernik]] says that Eblaite "is so closely related to Akkadian that it may be classified as an early Akkadian dialect", although some of the names that appear in the tablets are [[Northwest Semitic]].<ref>Krebernik, "Linguistic Classification"</ref>

=== North Semitic classification ===
*[[Edward Lipiński (orientalist)|Edward Lipiński]], claiming that in the third millennium BC, there was no clear border between [[East Semitic languages]] and [[West Semitic languages]], calls Eblaite "Paleosyrian" and explains the similarities to Akkadian by the use of the same system of writing borrowed from Sumer.{{sfn|Lipiński|2001|p=49}} Lipiński separates Eblaite from Akkadian, assigning the latter to the East Semitic languages while classifying Eblaite with Amorite and Ugaritic into a grouping he names the North Semitic languages.{{sfn|Lipiński|2001|p=50}}

By supporters of a classification as East Semitic, Eblaite is considered a language which exhibits both West Semitic and East Semitic features.<ref name="arol2">{{cite book|url= https://books.google.com/books?id=NffLn98SoIQC&pg=PA550|title= Semitic studies, Volume 1|author= Alan S. Kaye|page= 550|year= 1991|publisher= Otto Harrassowitz Verlag|isbn= 978-3-447-03168-4|url-status= live|archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20180320153250/https://books.google.com/books?id=NffLn98SoIQC&pg=PA550|archive-date= 2018-03-20}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|url= https://books.google.com/books?id=aWhHAQAAQBAJ&pg=PA101|title= The Semitic Languages|author= Robert Hetzron|page= 101|year= 2013|publisher= Routledge|isbn= 978-1-136-11580-6|url-status= live|archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20160423215104/https://books.google.com/books?id=aWhHAQAAQBAJ&pg=PA101|archive-date= 2016-04-23}}</ref> Grammatically, Eblaite is more similar to Akkadian, but lexically and in some grammatical forms, Eblaite is more similar to West Semitic languages.<ref>{{cite book|url= https://books.google.com/books?id=goq0VWw9rGIC&pg=PA226|title= Mercer Dictionary of the Bible|author= Watson E. Mills, Roger Aubrey Bullard|page= 226|year= 1990|publisher= Mercer University Press|isbn= 978-0-86554-373-7|url-status= live|archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20160521214518/https://books.google.com/books?id=goq0VWw9rGIC&pg=PA226|archive-date= 2016-05-21}}</ref>
